triage.name: Hypothyroidism
triage.reason: Common endocrine case with fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance and constipation; diagnosis reachable by history, exam and thyroid function tests.

demographics: Women are affected several times more often than men
Incidence increases with age, especially after age 60
More common in White and Hispanic populations than in Black populations in the US
Congenital hypothyroidism occurs in about 1 in 2,000–4,000 newborns

risk_factors.text: Family history of thyroid disease or autoimmune disease
Prior thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine treatment
External radiation to the neck or chest
Pregnancy or delivery within the past 6 months
Personal history of another autoimmune disease
Iodine deficiency or excess iodine intake

family_history: Graves' disease or other autoimmune thyroid disease
Other autoimmune disease (type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, celiac disease)
social_history: Low dietary iodine intake (rare in the US because of iodized salt)
High iodine intake from supplements, kelp, or contrast media
exposures: External beam radiation to the neck

chief_complaints.text: I've been gaining weight even though I'm not eating more
I just can't seem to get warm
My skin is so dry and my hair is thinning
My periods are heavier and irregular

hpi.onset: Gradual and insidious, often over months; many patients cannot pinpoint when it started
hpi.duration: Usually 6 months to several years of subtle symptoms before diagnosis
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; symptoms accumulate and worsen over time, and patients often attribute them to aging, stress, or being busy
hpi.quality: A generalized slowing: fatigue, cold intolerance, mental fog, and body changes rather than a discrete pain
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate at diagnosis; can be severe if untreated for a long time
hpi.timing: Constant, present every day; worse in cold weather and in the morning

associated_symptoms.text: Dry, thinning hair and hair loss
Puffy face, especially around the eyes

positives.text: Numbness or tingling in the hands

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms are often subtle and attributed to aging; patients may present mainly with cognitive slowing, depression, falls, or unexplained heart failure rather than classic cold intolerance and weight gain.

Symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy (fatigue, weight gain, constipation), so hypothyroidism is often found on screening rather than from complaints; untreated disease risks miscarriage, preterm birth, and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
missing_classic_features: Cold intolerance as a distinguishing feature

atypical.how_it_differs: Children may present with poor growth, delayed puberty, school problems, or a goiter; infants with congenital hypothyroidism are usually asymptomatic at birth and are detected by newborn screening, but may have prolonged jaundice, constipation, poor feeding, and hypotonia.
missing_classic_features: Classic adult fatigue and weight complaints

atypical.how_it_differs: Weight gain and fatigue are attributed to obesity itself, delaying diagnosis; hypothyroidism should be considered when these symptoms worsen or are accompanied by cold intolerance and constipation.
missing_classic_features: Weight gain as a distinguishing clue

general.mild: Alert, well-appearing but low-energy; may speak and move slowly
general.moderate: Noticeably slowed speech and movement, hoarse voice, puffy face, dry skin
general.severe: Ill-appearing, markedly slowed, hypothermic, periorbital and facial swelling, non-pitting edema
general.critical: Obtunded or comatose, hypothermic, bradycardic, hypoventilating (myxedema coma)

findings.maneuver: Auscultate the heart and palpate the radial pulse
findings.finding: Sinus bradycardia with a slow, regular rate

findings.maneuver: Tap the biceps, brachioradialis, or ankle reflex with a reflex hammer and watch the relaxation phase
findings.finding: Prolonged relaxation phase of the deep tendon reflexes (pseudomyotonia)

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the skin of the arms, legs, and trunk
findings.finding: Dry, coarse, cool skin with decreased sweating

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the pretibial area and the dorsum of the feet
findings.finding: Non-pitting (myxedematous) edema of the lower legs and feet

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face and periorbital area
findings.finding: Puffy face and periorbital edema

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to protrude the tongue and inspect it
findings.finding: Enlarged, thick tongue

findings.maneuver: Listen to the patient's voice during the interview
findings.finding: Hoarse, low-pitched, or slow speech

findings.maneuver: Inspect the neck and palpate the thyroid gland while the patient swallows
findings.finding: Diffusely enlarged, firm, non-tender thyroid (goiter), often in Hashimoto's thyroiditis
No thyroid tenderness

findings.maneuver: Palpate the thyroid gland for focal masses
findings.finding: No discrete dominant nodule

findings.maneuver: Palpate the cervical lymph node chains
findings.finding: No cervical lymphadenopathy
Clear breath sounds without crackles or wheeze

findings.maneuver: Auscultate bowel sounds and palpate the abdomen
findings.finding: Normal bowel sounds, soft, non-tender abdomen without organomegaly

findings.maneuver: Ask the patient to hold both arms outstretched with fingers spread
findings.finding: No fine tremor

findings.maneuver: Test proximal muscle strength (shoulder abduction, hip flexion)
findings.finding: Normal proximal strength without muscle wasting

findings.maneuver: Inspect the eyes for proptosis and lid retraction
findings.finding: No exophthalmos or lid lag

labs.caveat: Elevated TSH is the primary screening and diagnostic test in primary hypothyroidism. A normal TSH makes primary hypothyroidism very unlikely. In central (pituitary or hypothalamic) hypothyroidism TSH may be low, normal, or mildly elevated, so free T4 is needed.

Low free T4 with a high TSH confirms overt primary hypothyroidism. A normal free T4 with a high TSH is subclinical hypothyroidism. Low free T4 with a low or inappropriately normal TSH points to central hypothyroidism.
Hypothyroidism reduces LDL clearance and commonly raises total and LDL cholesterol; the lipid panel often improves after thyroid hormone replacement.
Mildly elevated CK from myopathy; marked elevation with muscle pain or weakness should raise concern for rhabdomyolysis, especially in myxedema coma.
Normocytic or macrocytic anemia; macrocytosis may also reflect coexisting pernicious anemia or celiac disease.
Hyponatremia is common in severe hypothyroidism and myxedema coma, from reduced free water clearance and sometimes coexisting adrenal insufficiency.
Mild rise from reduced renal perfusion and increased vascular resistance; usually improves with treatment.
Check before starting thyroid hormone when central hypothyroidism or myxedema coma is suspected; treating hypothyroidism before unrecognized adrenal insufficiency can precipitate an adrenal crisis.
Mildly elevated in Hashimoto's thyroiditis; marked elevation or neck pain suggests subacute thyroiditis instead.

findings.finding: Sinus bradycardia
Prolonged QT interval
Low-voltage QRS complexes from myxedematous pericardial effusion
Flattened or inverted T waves
First-degree AV block or bundle branch block
Sinus rhythm with occasional premature beats

imaging.preferred_when: Palpable thyroid nodule, asymmetric goiter, or concern for thyroid cancer

findings.text: Diffusely enlarged, heterogeneous thyroid with hypoechoic parenchyma (Hashimoto's thyroiditis)
Discrete thyroid nodule requiring further evaluation

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected pericardial effusion, unexplained heart failure, or severe hypothyroidism

findings.text: Pericardial effusion, usually small and without tamponade
Normal or mildly reduced systolic function with diastolic dysfunction

imaging.preferred_when: Rarely needed; used to distinguish causes of thyrotoxicosis rather than hypothyroidism

findings.text: Low or absent uptake in hypothyroidism from thyroiditis or exogenous hormone
Enlarged cardiac silhouette from pericardial effusion

initial.why: First-line test for suspected hypothyroidism; elevated TSH is the key finding in primary disease
Confirms overt hypothyroidism and distinguishes primary from central causes
Looks for the anemia that often accompanies hypothyroidism
Checks sodium and creatinine, which may be abnormal in severe disease
Hypothyroidism commonly raises cholesterol and triglycerides

supporting.why: Rules out adrenal insufficiency before starting thyroid hormone
supporting.only_if: central hypothyroidism or myxedema coma is suspected

supporting.why: Helps distinguish Hashimoto's thyroiditis from subacute thyroiditis
supporting.only_if: neck pain or a tender thyroid

supporting.why: Evaluates a nodule or asymmetric goiter
Assesses for pericardial effusion or cardiac dysfunction
supporting.only_if: suspected effusion, heart failure, or severe hypothyroidism

not_indicated.why: Used to evaluate thyrotoxicosis, not hypothyroidism
Rarely changes management unless a large effusion is suspected
No role in the evaluation of hypothyroidism

decision_points: A normal TSH makes primary hypothyroidism very unlikely; check free T4 when central hypothyroidism is suspected
Check morning cortisol before starting thyroid hormone if adrenal insufficiency could coexist
In myxedema coma, treat with thyroid hormone and stress-dose glucocorticoids while supporting ventilation and warming the patient

differential.name: Subclinical hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Mild fatigue, weight gain, and cold intolerance with an elevated TSH on screening

history: Symptoms are mild or absent
Often found on routine screening rather than from complaints
labs: Elevated TSH with a normal free T4

differential.name: Central hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Classic hypothyroid symptoms with low thyroid hormone levels
differential.trigger: Low free T4 with a low, normal, or only mildly elevated TSH

history: Headache, visual changes, or known pituitary disease
Symptoms of other pituitary hormone deficiencies (adrenal insufficiency, hypogonadism)
History of pituitary surgery or radiation
labs: Low or inappropriately normal TSH with low free T4
Low morning cortisol, low FSH/LH, low IGF-1

differential.name: Subacute (painless or painful) thyroiditis
differential.why_considered: Thyroid dysfunction with fatigue and neck discomfort

history: Recent viral illness
Neck pain radiating to the jaw or ear
Often a transient hyperthyroid phase before hypothyroidism
labs: Low TSH during the thyrotoxic phase, then elevated TSH later

differential.name: Hashimoto's thyroiditis
differential.why_considered: The most common cause of primary hypothyroidism, with fatigue, cold intolerance, and goiter

history: Gradual onset over months
Family history of autoimmune thyroid disease
Personal history of another autoimmune disease
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
imaging: Diffusely heterogeneous, hypoechoic thyroid on ultrasound

differential.name: Depression
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, low mood, poor concentration, and weight change

history: Pervasive low mood and anhedonia
Sleep and appetite changes
No cold intolerance or constipation

differential.name: Anemia
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, pallor, and reduced exercise tolerance

history: Pallor, exertional dyspnea, or bleeding
No cold intolerance or weight gain
labs: Low hemoglobin with normal TSH and free T4

differential.name: Obstructive sleep apnea
differential.why_considered: Daytime fatigue, snoring, and cognitive slowing

history: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas, morning headaches
No cold intolerance or constipation
Known kidney disease, hypertension, or diabetes
No cold intolerance
labs: Elevated creatinine and BUN with normal TSH and free T4

differential.name: Medication side effects
differential.why_considered: Fatigue, weight gain, and constipation from sedatives, beta blockers, or other drugs

history: Temporal link to starting a new medication
No cold intolerance or dry skin

severity.mild: Subclinical or early overt disease: mild fatigue, cold intolerance, and constipation with an elevated TSH and normal or borderline-low free T4
severity.moderate: Overt hypothyroidism: clear fatigue, weight gain, dry skin, bradycardia, and delayed reflexes with elevated TSH and low free T4
severity.severe: Marked hypothyroidism: hypothermia, bradycardia, non-pitting edema, hoarse voice, cognitive slowing, and possible pericardial effusion
severity.critical: Myxedema coma: obtundation or coma, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatremia, and hypotension

red_flags.meaning: Myxedema coma; needs ICU-level care and immediate thyroid hormone replacement
Severe hypothyroidism or myxedema coma; active warming and hormone replacement are needed
Cardiovascular collapse from severe hypothyroidism; monitor and support hemodynamics
Myxedema coma with respiratory depression; may require mechanical ventilation
Severe hypothyroidism with impaired free water clearance; correct sodium carefully

red_flags.finding: Low free T4 with low or normal TSH
red_flags.meaning: Central hypothyroidism; check cortisol before starting thyroid hormone to avoid precipitating adrenal crisis

complications.name: Pericardial effusion
clues: Enlarged cardiac silhouette on chest x-ray

complications.name: Carpal tunnel syndrome
clues: Numbness and tingling in the hands

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are often subtle and attributed to aging; may present with cognitive slowing, depression, falls, or unexplained heart failure rather than classic cold intolerance and weight gain.

Symptoms overlap with normal pregnancy, so screening is important; untreated hypothyroidism increases the risk of miscarriage, preterm birth, gestational hypertension, and impaired fetal neurodevelopment. Levothyroxine requirements often increase during pregnancy.

May present with poor growth, delayed puberty, school problems, or goiter; congenital hypothyroidism is usually asymptomatic at birth and is detected by newborn screening, but can cause prolonged jaundice, constipation, poor feeding, and hypotonia if missed.
Congenital hypothyroidism is typically identified on newborn screening; early treatment is critical to prevent irreversible neurodevelopmental impairment.
Weight gain and fatigue are attributed to obesity itself, delaying diagnosis; consider hypothyroidism when these symptoms worsen or are accompanied by cold intolerance and constipation.

key_questions.question: How has your energy level been over the past few months?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual, persistent fatigue and low energy over weeks to months

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any change in your weight, even though your appetite hasn't changed?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight gain despite unchanged or reduced appetite

key_questions.question: Do you feel cold when others around you are comfortable?
key_questions.looking_for: Cold intolerance, a fairly specific clue to hypothyroidism

key_questions.question: How often are you having bowel movements? Any constipation?
Have you noticed dry skin, thinning hair, or brittle nails?
key_questions.looking_for: Dry, coarse skin and hair thinning or loss

key_questions.question: Has your voice changed, or have you felt any fullness or swelling in your neck?
key_questions.looking_for: Hoarseness or a goiter suggesting thyroid enlargement

key_questions.question: How has your mood and thinking been? Any trouble concentrating or feeling down?
key_questions.looking_for: Depressed mood, slowed thinking, or memory problems

key_questions.question: Have your menstrual periods changed in flow or regularity?
key_questions.looking_for: Heavy or irregular periods, or difficulty conceiving

key_questions.question: Have you had any palpitations, racing heart, heat intolerance, or unintentional weight loss?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; their presence points toward hyperthyroidism instead

key_questions.question: Have you ever had thyroid surgery, radioactive iodine, or radiation to the neck or chest?
key_questions.looking_for: Prior thyroid ablation or surgery, a strong cause of hypothyroidism

key_questions.question: Do you take any medications such as amiodarone, lithium, or interferon, or have you had recent iodinated contrast?
key_questions.looking_for: Drugs that can cause or worsen hypothyroidism

key_questions.question: Does anyone in your family have thyroid disease or another autoimmune condition?
key_questions.looking_for: Family history of Hashimoto's thyroiditis, Graves' disease, or other autoimmune disease

key_questions.question: Do you have any other autoimmune conditions such as type 1 diabetes, celiac disease, or pernicious anemia?
key_questions.looking_for: Coexisting autoimmune disease raising suspicion for Hashimoto's thyroiditis

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant, or have you delivered a baby in the past 6 months?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy or recent delivery, which raises risk and changes management

key_questions.question: Have you had any confusion, severe drowsiness, or been told you were very cold or slow to wake?
key_questions.looking_for: Altered mental status or hypothermia suggesting myxedema coma

reasoning_points: Gradual onset over months of fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, and dry skin
Risk factors such as female sex, older age, family history of thyroid or autoimmune disease, prior thyroid surgery or radiation, and medications like amiodarone or lithium
Exam findings of bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, dry coarse skin, and possibly a non-tender goiter
Elevated TSH with low free T4 confirming overt primary hypothyroidism
Positive thyroid peroxidase antibodies supporting Hashimoto's thyroiditis as the cause
Look-alikes such as depression, anemia, obstructive sleep apnea, and chronic kidney disease excluded by history and normal thyroid function tests
Red flags for myxedema coma (altered mental status, hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, hyponatremia) recognized and treated urgently
Central hypothyroidism considered when free T4 is low with a low or inappropriately normal TSH, with cortisol checked before starting thyroid hormone

easy: Middle-aged woman with classic fatigue, cold intolerance, weight gain, and constipation
Bradycardia and delayed deep tendon reflexes on exam
Elevated TSH with low free T4 on labs
Known Hashimoto's thyroiditis or prior thyroid surgery
medium: Older adult whose symptoms are attributed to aging, presenting with cognitive slowing or depression
Patient with a non-tender goiter and nonspecific complaints
Coexisting anemia or dyslipidemia that partially explains the symptoms
Pregnancy with fatigue and weight gain overlapping normal pregnancy symptoms
hard: Subclinical hypothyroidism with an elevated TSH but normal free T4 and minimal symptoms
Central hypothyroidism with low free T4 and a low or normal TSH
Myxedema coma presenting with altered mental status, hypothermia, and hypoventilation
Child with poor growth or delayed puberty and few classic adult features
Symptoms attributed to obesity, delaying the diagnosis
